Get started with zuregex

Source: vignettes/zuregex.Rmd
zuregex.Rmd
library(zuregex)

We take a few lines of a web server’s log and work through them: find the lines that match, pull out parts of them, turn them into a data frame, rewrite them and cut them up. After that you know the main re_*() functions and the rules they share. Moving from base R or stringr, limits on untrusted patterns and the C API each have their own article, listed at the end.

Detect matches

The log is a character vector. Its last element is not a log line, so we can see what a string that does not match gives.

log <- c(
  "2026-10-21 08:15:02 GET /index.html 200 512",
  "2026-10-21 08:15:09 POST /login 302 0",
  "2026-10-21 08:16:44 GET /missing 404 128",
  "not a log line"
)

Every function takes the strings first, as x, and then a pattern: a regular expression in PCRE2’s syntax, which is the syntax of base R’s perl = TRUE. re_detect() says which elements match.

re_detect(log, "GET")
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

One pattern is used for every element. The other choice is one pattern per element, as long as x. Here each line is tested for its own status code, and only the second line has the one asked for.

re_detect(log, c("404", "302", "200", "500"))
#> [1] FALSE  TRUE FALSE FALSE

A pattern of any other length is an error: zuregex never recycles one.

Extract matches

re_extract() returns the text of the first match in each element, and NA where there is none.

re_extract(log, "/\\S+")
#> [1] "/index.html" "/login"      "/missing"    NA

Parentheses in a pattern make a group, a part of the match you can ask for by itself. group picks one, by number or, for a group written (?<name>...), by name. This returns the status code alone, without the spaces the pattern needs around it.

re_extract(log, " (?<status>\\d{3}) ", group = "status")
#> [1] "200" "302" "404" NA

Capture groups as columns

re_match() returns every group at once, as a data frame with one row per element. A named group gives its name to its column.

pattern <- "(?<time>\\S+ \\S+) (?<method>[A-Z]+) (?<path>\\S+) (?<status>\\d+)"
re_match(log, pattern)
#>                  time method        path status
#> 1 2026-10-21 08:15:02    GET /index.html    200
#> 2 2026-10-21 08:15:09   POST      /login    302
#> 3 2026-10-21 08:16:44    GET    /missing    404
#> 4                <NA>   <NA>        <NA>   <NA>

The columns are character. proto gives them types, as it does for utils::strcapture(): a data frame whose columns are examples of the type wanted. Look at status, now an integer.

proto <- data.frame(time = "", method = "", path = "", status = 0L)
str(re_match(log, pattern, proto = proto))
#> 'data.frame':    4 obs. of  4 variables:
#>  $ time  : chr  "2026-10-21 08:15:02" "2026-10-21 08:15:09" "2026-10-21 08:16:44" NA
#>  $ method: chr  "GET" "POST" "GET" NA
#>  $ path  : chr  "/index.html" "/login" "/missing" NA
#>  $ status: int  200 302 404 NA

re_match() looks at the first match in each element. re_match_all() returns a row for every match, with element and match saying where each came from. Each of the first three lines has two numbers at its end, and the last line has no rows.

re_match_all(log, " (?<number>\\d+)(?= |$)")
#>   element match number
#> 1       1     1    200
#> 2       1     2    512
#> 3       2     1    302
#> 4       2     2      0
#> 5       3     1    404
#> 6       3     2    128

Replace and split

re_replace() replaces every match with a template, in which ${name} or $1 stands for a group. Here the date is turned round, and the line with no date comes back unchanged.

re_replace(log, "^(?<y>\\d+)-(?<m>\\d+)-(?<d>\\d+)", "${d}/${m}/${y}")
#> [1] "21/10/2026 08:15:02 GET /index.html 200 512"
#> [2] "21/10/2026 08:15:09 POST /login 302 0"      
#> [3] "21/10/2026 08:16:44 GET /missing 404 128"   
#> [4] "not a log line"

Templates can do more than this, such as defaults and case changes; ?re_replace lists the syntax.

re_split() cuts each element at the matches, and returns a list with a character vector of pieces per element.

re_split(log[1:2], " ")
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "2026-10-21"  "08:15:02"    "GET"         "/index.html" "200"        
#> [6] "512"        
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "2026-10-21" "08:15:09"   "POST"       "/login"     "302"       
#> [6] "0"

Compile a pattern once

So far each pattern was a string. re_compile() turns one into an re object, which carries its flags with it and which every function takes in place of the string. The flag i ignores case, so this lower-case pattern finds the log’s GET.

get <- re_compile("\\bget\\b", flags = "i")
get
#> <re[1]>
#> [1] /\bget\b/i
re_detect(log, get)
#> [1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

You do not need re_compile() for speed. Pattern strings go through a cache, so a string used again is not compiled again; see ?re_cache_size.

When a pattern is wrong

The most common mistake is a pattern that is not valid. This one never closes the group it opens.

re_match(log, "(?<time>\\S+ \\S+ (?<method>[A-Z]+)")
#> Error in `re_match()`:
#> ! Can't compile pattern: missing closing parenthesis at character 34.
#>   (?<time>\S+ \S+ (?<method>[A-Z]+)
#>                                    ^

The error names the problem and marks where in the pattern PCRE2 found it. Like every error zuregex raises, it has a class, here zuregex_error_compile, so tryCatch() can handle it.
